q: In which year was the Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act implemented?
e: The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act was implemented in 1972 with various provisions for protecting habitats.

q: In which year was "Project Tiger" launched in India?
e: Project Tiger, one of the well-publicised wildlife campaigns in the world, was launched in 1973.

q: Which famous movement in the Himalayas successfully resisted deforestation and promoted community afforestation?
e: The famous Chipko movement in the Himalayas successfully resisted deforestation in several areas and showed that community afforestation with indigenous species can be enormously successful.

q: Which category of forests is regarded as the most valuable as far as the conservation of forest and wildlife resources is concerned?
e: More than half of the total forest land has been declared reserved forests and they are regarded as the most valuable for conservation.

q: Which state passed the first formal resolution for Joint Forest Management (JFM) in 1988?
e: The Joint Forest Management (JFM) programme came into formal existence in 1988 when the state of Odisha passed the first resolution.

q: In which Indian state is Corbett National Park (Tiger Reserve) located?
e: Corbett National Park is a major tiger reserve located in Uttarakhand.

q: In which state is Sundarbans National Park located?
e: Sundarbans National Park is located in West Bengal.

q: Which two trees are worshipped by the Mundas and the Santhals of Chota Nagpur region?
e: The Mundas and the Santhals of Chota Nagpur region worship mahua (Bassia latifolia) and kadamba (Anthocephalus cadamba) trees.

q: Which state has the largest area under permanent forests in India?
e: Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests, constituting 75 per cent of its total forest area.

q: In which state is Bandhavgarh National Park situated?
e: Bandhavgarh National Park is located in Madhya Pradesh.

q: In which state is Manas Tiger Reserve located?
e: Manas Tiger Reserve is located in Assam.

q: In which state is Periyar Tiger Reserve located?
e: Periyar Tiger Reserve is located in Kerala.

q: In which state is Sariska Wildlife Sanctuary / Tiger Reserve located?
e: Sariska Tiger Reserve is located in Rajasthan, where villagers fought against mining.

q: Around the Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan, herds of which animals are seen as an integral part of the community and nobody harms them?
e: In and around Bishnoi villages in Rajasthan, herds of blackbuck (chinkara), nilgai and peacocks can be seen as an integral part of the community.

q: Which farmers’ movement in Tehri demonstrated adequate levels of diversified crop production without using synthetic chemicals?
e: Farmers and citizen’s groups like the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible and economically viable.

q: Approximately what percentage of the total volume of world’s water is estimated to exist as fresh water?
e: About 96.5 per cent of the total volume of world’s water exists as oceans and only 2.5 per cent is fresh water.

q: Who proudly proclaimed dams as the "temples of modern India"?
e: Jawaharlal Nehru proudly proclaimed the dams as the "temples of modern India" for integrating agriculture with rapid industrialisation and growth.

q: On which river is the Hirakud Dam built?
e: The Hirakud project in the Mahanadi basin integrates conservation of water with flood control.

q: On which river is the Sardar Sarovar Dam built?
e: Sardar Sarovar Dam has been built over the Narmada River in Gujarat, covering Maharashtra, MP, Gujarat and Rajasthan.

q: On which river basin is the Bhakra-Nangal project located?
e: In the Sutlej-Beas river basin, the Bhakra-Nangal project water is used both for hydel power production and irrigation.

q: Which is the first state in India that has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structures compulsory to all the houses across the state?
e: Tamil Nadu is the first state in India which has made rooftop rainwater harvesting structure compulsory to all the houses across the state.

q: In hill and mountainous regions of the Western Himalayas, people built diversion channels for agriculture known as:
e: In hill and mountainous regions, people built diversion channels like the "guls" or "kuls" of the Western Himalayas for agriculture.

q: In semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan (Bikaner, Phalodi, Barmer), underground tanks built in houses for storing drinking water are called:
e: In semi-arid and arid regions of Rajasthan like Bikaner, Phalodi and Barmer, almost all houses traditionally had underground tanks or "tankas" for storing drinking water.

q: What is rainwater commonly referred to in parts of Rajasthan, considered the purest form of natural water?
e: Rain water, or "palar pani" as commonly referred to in these parts of Rajasthan, is considered the purest form of natural water.

q: Who constructed the tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi in the 14th century for supplying water to the Siri Fort area?
e: In the 14th century, the tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi was constructed by Iltutmish for supplying water to Siri Fort area.

q: In which state is the 200-year-old Bamboo Drip Irrigation system practised?
e: In Meghalaya, a 200-year-old system of tapping stream and spring water by using bamboo pipes is prevalent.

q: In which state is Gendathur village (famous for nearly 200 households installing rooftop rainwater harvesting) located?
e: In Gendathur, a remote backward village in Mysuru, Karnataka, villagers have installed rooftop rainwater harvesting systems in nearly 200 households.

q: In Jaisalmer, rain-fed storage structures allowing water to stand and moisten the soil in agricultural fields are known as:
e: In arid/semi-arid regions, agricultural fields were converted into rain-fed storage structures known as "Khadins" in Jaisalmer and "Johads" in other parts of Rajasthan.

q: What is the main goal of the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) announced by the Government of India?
o: Enable every rural household to get assured supply of potable piped water at a service level of 55 litres per capita per day regularly
Supply water solely to IT parks
e: The goal of JJM is to enable every rural household to get assured supply of potable piped water at a service level of 55 litres per capita per day regularly on a long-term basis.

q: How does nearly every household in Shillong (Meghalaya) cope with acute water shortage despite being close to Cherrapunji?
o: By having a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure
e: Nearly every household in Shillong has a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure, meeting nearly 15–25 per cent of the total water requirement of the household.

q: Which of the following statements is NOT a valid reason for the depletion of flora and fauna? [JAC PYQ]
e: Per NCERT, many environmentalists note that grazing and fuel-wood collection in traditional rural forms (often lopping rather than felling whole trees) is not the main cause compared to commercial expansion, projects and urbanisation.

q: Which of the following conservation strategies do NOT directly involve community participation? [JAC PYQ]
e: Demarcation of wildlife sanctuaries is a government/administrative action rather than a direct community-led conservation strategy.

q: Which one of the following statements is NOT an argument in favour of multi-purpose river projects? [JAC PYQ]
o: Multi-purpose projects bring water to those areas which suffer from water scarcity
Multi-purpose projects by regulating water flow help to control floods
Multi-purpose projects lead to large scale displacements and loss of livelihood
Multi-purpose projects generate electricity for our industries and homes
e: Large scale displacement and loss of livelihood is a major argument AGAINST multi-purpose river projects, not in favour of them.

q: Which aspect of water scarcity is related to qualitative deterioration rather than sheer absence of rainfall?
o: Sufficient water availability in an area yet polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals and pesticides
e: Qualitative scarcity occurs when water is sufficiently available to meet needs, yet polluted by domestic and industrial wastes, chemicals, pesticides and fertilisers making it hazardous for human use.

q: By 1973, the tiger population in India had dwindled to roughly what number from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the century?
e: In 1973, authorities realised that the tiger population had dwindled to 1,827 from an estimated 55,000 at the turn of the century.

q: Under the Wildlife Act of 1980 and 1986, which smaller organisms were added to the list of protected species?
o: Several hundred butterflies, moths, beetles, and one dragonfly
e: Under the Wildlife Act of 1980 and 1986, several hundred butterflies, moths, beetles, and one dragonfly were added to protected species; in 1991, plants were also added starting with six species.

q: Reserved and protected forests are collectively referred to as what?
e: Reserved and protected forests are also referred to as permanent forest estates maintained for the purpose of producing timber and other forest produce, and for protective reasons.

q: Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan have a bulk of their forests under which category?
e: Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Himachal Pradesh, Odisha and Rajasthan have a bulk of their forests under protected forests.

q: Inhabitants of five villages in Alwar district of Rajasthan declared 1,200 hectares of forest as what, with their own rules banning hunting?
e: Villagers in Alwar district of Rajasthan declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav "Sonchuri", declaring their own rules disallowing hunting and protecting wildlife.

q: In the 1st century B.C., which place near Allahabad had a sophisticated water harvesting system channelling the flood water of the river Ganga?
e: In the first century B.C., Sringaverapura near Allahabad had a sophisticated water harvesting system channelling the flood water of the river Ganga.

q: In India, hydroelectric power contributes approximately what percentage of the total electricity produced?
e: In India, hydroelectric power contributes approximately 22 per cent of the total electricity produced.

q: Of the world’s freshwater, nearly what percentage occurs as ice sheets and glaciers in Antarctica, Greenland and mountainous regions?
e: Nearly 70 per cent of the world’s freshwater occurs as ice sheets and glaciers, while a little less than 30 per cent is stored as groundwater.

q: The Krishna-Godavari water dispute arose due to objections raised by which states against the diversion of water at Koyna by the Maharashtra government?
e: Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh governments objected regarding the diversion of more water at Koyna by the Maharashtra government for a multipurpose project, reducing downstream flow.

q: Which artificial lake built in the 11th century was one of the largest of its time?
e: In the 11th Century, Bhopal Lake, one of the largest artificial lakes of its time, was built.

q: Despite being just 55 km from Cherrapunji and Mawsynram, which state capital faces acute shortage of water?
e: Shillong is situated just 55 km from Cherrapunji and Mawsynram (wettest places), yet the state capital faces acute shortage of water.

q: The tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship which two trees during weddings?
e: The tribals of Odisha and Bihar worship the tamarind (Tamarindus indica) and mango (Mangifera indica) trees during weddings.

q: Which region of India has a very high percentage of its forests as unclassed forests managed by local communities?
o: All North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat
e: All North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat have a very high percentage of their forests as unclassed forests managed by local communities.

q: Who did the Narmada Bachao Andolan (an NGO) mobilise against the Sardar Sarovar Dam?
o: Tribal people, farmers, environmentalists and human rights activists
e: Narmada Bachao Andolan is a Non Governmental Organisation (NGO) that mobilised tribal people, farmers, environmentalists and human rights activists against the Sardar Sarovar Dam.

q: In Meghalaya’s bamboo drip irrigation system, 18-20 litres of water entering the bamboo pipe system gets reduced at the site of the plant to:
e: About 18-20 litres of water enters the bamboo pipe system, gets transported over hundreds of metres, and finally reduces to 20-80 drops per minute at the site of the plant.

q: Which river basin is served by the Damodar Valley project (with reservoirs like Tilaiya, Maithon, Panchet)?
o: Damodar river basin (Jharkhand and West Bengal)
e: Damodar Valley project is a multi-purpose river valley project across Jharkhand and West Bengal controlling floods and generating hydel power in the Damodar basin.

q: Besides drinking water, what extra benefit did underground room tanks (tankas) provide in Rajasthan houses during summers?
o: Underground rooms adjoining the tanka stayed cool and beat the summer heat
e: Many houses constructed underground rooms adjoining the "tanka" to beat the summer heat as it would keep the room cool.

q: Evidence of what ancient infrastructure has been found at Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka) and Kolhapur (Maharashtra)?
e: Evidence of sophisticated irrigation works has also been found in Kalinga (Odisha), Nagarjunakonda (Andhra Pradesh), Bennur (Karnataka), Kolhapur (Maharashtra), etc.

q: How does damming of rivers adversely affect aquatic fauna?
o: Dams fragment rivers making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning
e: Dams fragment rivers making it difficult for aquatic fauna to migrate, especially for spawning.

q: Why is the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting on the decline in western Rajasthan today?
o: Plenty of water is available due to the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal
e: Today, in western Rajasthan, sadly the practice of rooftop rainwater harvesting is on the decline as plenty of water is available due to the perennial Indira Gandhi Canal.

q: Roughly what fraction of the total forest area in India falls under "Protected Forests"?
e: Almost one-third of the total forest area is protected forest, as declared by the Forest Department, protected from any further depletion.

q: Nagarjuna Sagar Dam is built on which river?
e: Nagarjuna Sagar Dam is a major multi-purpose project built across the Krishna River.

q: Which group of Indian states has large percentages of RESERVED forests of their total forest area?
o: Jammu & Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal and Maharashtra
e: Jammu and Kashmir, Andhra Pradesh, Uttarakhand, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, West Bengal, and Maharashtra have large percentages of reserved forests of their total forest area.

q: Which major threats posed danger to the tiger population prompting Project Tiger in 1973?
o: Poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey base species and growing human population
e: Major threats to tiger population included poaching for trade, shrinking habitat, depletion of prey base species, growing human population, and illegal trade of skins and bones.

q: Which Act did villagers in Sariska Tiger Reserve (Rajasthan) cite while fighting against mining?
e: In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers have fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act.

q: The Sardar Sarovar Dam on the Narmada river covers water needs across which four states?
o: Gujarat, Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan
e: Sardar Sarovar Project is one of the largest water resource projects of India covering four states—Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat and Rajasthan.

q: Which of the following Dam–State pairs is correctly matched?
e: Hirakud (Odisha on Mahanadi) is correct; Salal is in J&K (Chenab), Mettur in Tamil Nadu (Kaveri), and Tehri in Uttarakhand (Bhagirathi).

q: Under Joint Forest Management (JFM), what incentive do local village communities receive in return for protecting degraded forests?
o: Intermediary benefits like non-timber forest produces and share in the timber harvested by successful protection
Absolute private title to forest land
e: JFM depends on local institutions protecting degraded forest land; in return, members are entitled to intermediary benefits like non-timber forest produces and share in timber harvested by "successful protection".

q: Why do densely populated Indian cities often face acute water scarcity even in regions that receive ample annual rainfall?
o: Due to rapid urbanisation, industrial demand, private groundwater pumping devices and pollution of water sources
e: Multiplying urban centres with large populations, urban lifestyles, industrial water/power demands, private groundwater pumping devices in housing colonies, and chemical/domestic pollution drive urban water scarcity.

q: Identify the INCORRECT match between Tiger Reserve and State:
e: Sundarbans National Park is located in West Bengal, not Odisha. All other pairs are correct.

q: How can large dams constructed to control floods paradoxically trigger floods during heavy rains?
o: Sedimentation in the reservoir reduces storage capacity, forcing sudden water release during excessive rain
e: Sedimentation in reservoirs reduces capacity and dams constructed to control floods have triggered floods; excessive water release during heavy rains in 2006 aggravated floods in Maharashtra and Gujarat.

q: In Rajasthan’s rooftop rainwater harvesting system, why is the water from the first spell of rain usually NOT collected in the tanka?
o: It is used to clean the roofs and the pipes
e: The first spell of rain is usually not collected as this would clean the roofs and the pipes; the rainwater from the subsequent showers is then collected.

q: How is each household in Gendathur village able to harvest about 50,000 litres of rainwater annually?
o: Gendathur receives ~1,000 mm annual precipitation and with ~80% collection efficiency across about 10 fillings collects ~50,000 litres
e: With an annual precipitation of 1,000 mm, 80% collection efficiency and about 10 fillings, every house can collect and use about 50,000 litres of water annually.

q: What long-term crisis is being created by farmers having their own wells and tube-wells in farms for irrigation?
o: Groundwater levels are falling adversely affecting water availability and food security
e: Excessive use of personal wells and tube-wells to expand irrigated area during dry seasons is causing groundwater levels to fall, threatening water availability and food security.

q: How do "Sacred groves" contribute to biodiversity conservation in India?
o: They are auctioned by Forest Dept
Protected due to traditional beliefs as forests of Gods/Goddesses, keeping patches virgin and untouched by human interference
Only single monoculture species are planted
e: Nature worship is an age-old tribal belief protecting virgin forests called Sacred Groves (forests of God and Goddesses); these patches have been left untouched by local people and any interference is banned.

q: Why was "enrichment plantation" practised by foresters considered harmful to biodiversity?
o: Because a single commercially valuable species was extensively planted while eliminating other native species
e: In enrichment plantation, a single commercially valuable species was extensively planted and other species eliminated—e.g. teak monoculture damaged natural forests in South India and Chir Pine replaced Himalayan oak and Rhododendron forests.

q: In the flood plains of Bengal, how did people traditionally irrigate their fields?
e: In the flood plains of Bengal, people developed inundation channels to irrigate their fields.

q: How does damming rivers affect the natural soil fertility of downstream flood plains?
o: Dams hold back sediment in reservoirs, depriving downstream flood plains of natural fertile silt and increasing land degradation
e: Damming affects natural flow causing poorer sediment flow and excessive sedimentation at the bottom of the reservoir; the flood plains are deprived of silt, a natural fertiliser, further adding to land degradation.

q: How has irrigation facilitated by multi-purpose dams changed the cropping pattern in many regions of India?
o: Farmers shifted to water-intensive and commercial crops, leading to ecological consequences like salinisation of the soil
e: Irrigation has changed the cropping pattern of many regions with farmers shifting to water-intensive and commercial crops, creating great ecological consequences like salinisation of the soil.

q: How does the Sardar Sarovar Project specifically benefit drought-prone regions of Gujarat and Rajasthan?
o: It meets water requirements of drought-prone and desert areas of Gujarat (9,490 villages, 173 towns) and Rajasthan (124 villages)
It produces only hydro power in Rajasthan
It connects Thar to Arabian Sea
e: The Sardar Sarovar project meets the requirement of water in drought-prone and desert areas of Gujarat (9,490 villages and 173 towns) and Rajasthan (124 villages).

q: Multi-purpose projects often trigger local inter-user conflicts within a region. Which example illustrates this from NCERT?
o: Agitation by Sabarmati-basin farmers in Gujarat when higher priority was given to water supply in urban areas during a drought
e: In Gujarat, Sabarmati-basin farmers were agitated and almost caused a riot over the higher priority given to water supply in urban areas, particularly during droughts.

q: Arrange these Tiger Reserves in India from NORTH to SOUTH: 1. Corbett, 2. Bandhavgarh, 3. Periyar
e: Corbett (Uttarakhand, North) → Bandhavgarh (Madhya Pradesh, Central) → Periyar (Kerala, South).

q: Arrange the following multi-purpose river projects from NORTH to SOUTH:
o: Salal → Bhakra-Nangal → Sardar Sarovar → Nagarjuna Sagar
Nagarjuna Sagar → Sardar Sarovar → Bhakra-Nangal → Salal
Bhakra-Nangal → Nagarjuna Sagar → Salal → Sardar Sarovar
Sardar Sarovar → Salal → Bhakra-Nangal → Nagarjuna Sagar
e: Salal (J&K) → Bhakra-Nangal (HP/Punjab) → Sardar Sarovar (Gujarat) → Nagarjuna Sagar (Andhra/Telangana).

q: Which post-1951 developmental activity alone cleared over 5,000 sq km of forest in India?
e: Since 1951, over 5,000 sq km of forest was cleared for river valley projects; clearing of forests is still continuing with projects like the Narmada Sagar Project in Madhya Pradesh.

q: Why is biodiversity essential for human survival?
o: Plants, animals and micro-organisms re-create the quality of air we breathe, water we drink and soil that produces our food
e: Forests play a key role in the ecological system as primary producers; plants, animals and micro-organisms recreate the quality of the air we breathe, the water we drink and the soil that produces our food.

q: How does traditional worship of mahua, kadamba, tamarind and mango in Chota Nagpur, Odisha and Bihar benefit ecology?
o: It ensures intergenerational conservation of these indigenous trees and associated biodiversity
e: Worship of mahua, kadamba, tamarind and mango trees by tribes in Chota Nagpur, Odisha and Bihar embeds biodiversity conservation into cultural traditions.

q: Why do housing societies and colonies in cities often worsen groundwater depletion?
o: Most colonies have their own groundwater pumping devices to meet water needs, and paved surfaces check percolation
e: Most housing societies or colonies in cities have their own groundwater pumping devices to meet their water needs, leading to over-exploitation and depletion of fragile groundwater resources.

q: What lesson does NCERT draw when comparing water availability in Cherrapunji–Shillong with western Rajasthan’s tanka culture?
o: High annual rainfall alone is insufficient without water management and conservation, whereas arid regions thrived via rainwater harvesting
Rooftop harvesting is impossible in hills
e: Even Shillong near the wettest spots relies on rooftop harvesting, while dry Rajasthan survived via tankas and khadins—proving conservation and management determine water security.

q:
Match the traditional rainwater harvesting structure with its region:
A. Guls/Kuls — 1. Rajasthan
B. Khadins/Johads — 2. Western Himalayas
C. Inundation channels — 3. Flood plains of Bengal
e: Guls/Kuls = Western Himalayas (A-2); Khadins/Johads = Rajasthan (B-1); Inundation channels = Bengal flood plains (C-3).

q: According to NCERT, on what bases are dams classified into categories like timber dams, embankment dams, or large dams?
o: According to structure and materials used, as well as height
e: Dams are classified according to structure and the materials used (timber, embankment, masonry) or intended purpose and height (large, major, medium/low dams).

q: Which forest category includes other forests and wastelands belonging to both government and private individuals and communities?
e: Unclassed forests are other forests and wastelands belonging to both government and private individuals and communities.

q: Ongoing mining of which mineral posed a serious threat to the Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal, disturbing natural habitats?
e: The Buxa Tiger Reserve in West Bengal has been seriously threatened by the ongoing dolomite mining, blocking migration routes of several species including the great Indian elephant.

q: Why is rainwater harvesting regarded as a viable alternative to large multi-purpose river projects in many Indian regions?
o: It is both socio-economically and environmentally viable without causing mass displacement or ecological disruption
e: Given the disadvantages and rising resistance against multi-purpose projects, water harvesting systems are considered a viable alternative both socio-economically and environmentally.

q: What common principle unites Meghalaya’s bamboo drip irrigation and Rajasthan’s rooftop tankas?
o: Both are indigenous traditional technologies finely adapted to local topography and hydrological conditions
e: People in ancient/traditional India had in-depth knowledge of rainfall regimes and soil types and developed wide ranging techniques adapted to local ecological conditions.

q: How does rapid industrialisation exert a double pressure on India’s existing freshwater resources?
o: Industries are heavy users of water and also require hydro-power to run them, while industrial wastes pollute freshwater
Industries create water from thin air
e: Industries, apart from being heavy users of water, also require power to run them (much of which comes from hydroelectric power) and contaminate water bodies with industrial effluents.

q: Why was international collaboration (such as India and Nepal together) highlighted as crucial under Project Tiger?
o: Because India and Nepal provide habitat to about two-thirds of the surviving tiger population in the world and became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading
Because tigers live only on glacier peaks
e: Since India and Nepal provide habitat to about two-thirds of the surviving tiger population in the world, these two nations became prime targets for poaching and illegal trading.

q:
Assertion (A): Tiger conservation in India is not only an effort to save an endangered species, but with equal importance as a means of preserving biotypes of sizeable magnitude.
Reason (R): Conservation projects are now focusing on biodiversity rather than on a few of its components.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Conservation strategies now focus on biodiversity as a whole and preserving large biotypes rather than isolated species.

q:
Assertion (A): In arid regions of Rajasthan, underground "tankas" are built inside houses to store drinking water.
Reason (R): Tankas are connected to sloping roofs via pipes to store rainwater ("palar pani"), providing reliable drinking water till the next rainy season.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are true and Reason (R) accurately explains how rooftop-connected tankas store palar pani till the next monsoon.

q:
Assertion (A): Joint Forest Management (JFM) came into formal existence in 1988 with the first resolution passed by the state of Punjab.
Reason (R): JFM depends on the formation of local village institutions that undertake protection activities on degraded forest land.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because the first JFM resolution in 1988 was passed by Odisha (not Punjab); Reason (R) is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Tamil Nadu is the first state in India which has made rooftop rainwater harvesting compulsory to all houses across the state.
Reason (R): There are no legal provisions to punish defaulters under this rule.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is true, while Reason (R) is false because Tamil Nadu indeed has legal provisions to punish the defaulters.

q:
Assertion (A): Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya have shown that diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals is possible and viable.
Reason (R): Madhya Pradesh has the largest area under permanent forests in India.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are independently true, yet Madhya Pradesh’s forest area does not explain the Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri.

q:
Assertion (A): Excessive sedimentation at the bottom of dam reservoirs can aggravate flood situations during heavy rainfall.
Reason (R): Reduced storage capacity forces authorities to release huge quantities of water during excessive rains, inundating downstream areas.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Sedimentation lowers storage capacity, triggering forced water releases and worsening downstream floods; R correctly explains A.

q:
Assertion (A): The Mundas and Santhals of Chota Nagpur region worship mahua and kadamba trees.
Reason (R): Nature worship is an age-old tribal belief in India based on the premise that all creations of nature have to be protected.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Age-old tribal traditions of nature worship directly explain why Mundas and Santhals revere and protect mahua and kadamba trees.

q:
Assertion (A): About 96.5 per cent of Earth’s water is in oceans and only 2.5 per cent exists as fresh water.
Reason (R): Nearly 70 per cent of that fresh water is locked in ice sheets and glaciers, making readily usable freshwater very limited.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements state accurate hydrological proportions, though R describes freshwater lock-up rather than why oceans hold 96.5%.

q:
Assertion (A): Shillong, capital of Meghalaya, needs no rainwater harvesting because it is near the wettest places on Earth.
Reason (R): Actually, Shillong faces an acute shortage of water and nearly every household there has a rooftop rainwater harvesting structure.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because Shillong actually suffers acute water shortage; Reason (R) is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Reserved forests are regarded as the most valuable as far as the conservation of forest and wildlife resources is concerned.
Reason (R): More than half of India’s total forest land has been declared reserved forests.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are true facts, though their >50% share is not by itself the explanation for why reserved forests are strictly protected as most valuable.

q:
Assertion (A): The Krishna-Godavari dispute originated with objections raised by Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh governments.
Reason (R): They objected to Maharashtra’s diversion of more water at Koyna, which would reduce downstream flow with adverse consequences for agriculture and industry.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are true and Reason (R) clearly explains the downstream concern driving the Krishna-Godavari dispute.

q:
Assertion (A): Commercial teak monoculture extensively helped enrich natural biodiversity in South India.
Reason (R): Actually, enrichment plantation of a single commercially valuable species eliminated other native species and damaged natural forests.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because teak monoculture damaged natural forests in South India; Reason (R) is true.

q:
Assertion (A): Irrigation from multi-purpose dams has shifted cropping patterns towards water-intensive and commercial crops.
Reason (R): This shift has led to ecological consequences like salinisation of the soil.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are true, but soil salinisation is a consequence of shifting to water-intensive crops rather than its cause.

q:
Assertion (A): The Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act of 1972 banned hunting, restricted wildlife trade and gave legal protection to habitats.
Reason (R): Later in 1991, for the first time plants were also added to the protected list starting with six species.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements accurately describe phases of wildlife legislation, though the 1991 amendment does not explain the 1972 provisions.

q:
Assertion (A): Jawaharlal Nehru proudly proclaimed dams as the "temples of modern India".
Reason (R): He believed dams would integrate the development of agriculture and village economy with rapid industrialisation and growth of the urban economy.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Reason (R) directly captures Jawaharlal Nehru’s rationale behind calling dams the "temples of modern India".

q:
Assertion (A): Villagers of five villages in Alwar district declared 1,200 hectares of forest as Bhairodev Dakav "Sonchuri" banning hunting.
Reason (R): All local rural communities in India view forests only as government property to be cleared indiscriminately.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is true, while Reason (R) is completely false as local communities actively protect forests and wildlife.

q:
Assertion (A): North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat have a high percentage of their forests as unclassed forests.
Reason (R): These unclassed forests are largely managed by local communities.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are factually true regarding unclassed forests in North-eastern states and Gujarat.

q:
Assertion (A): Conservation initiatives like Project Tiger were crucial for India and Nepal.
Reason (R): Together, India and Nepal harbour only about 5 per cent of the world’s surviving tiger population.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is true, while Reason (R) is false because India and Nepal together provide habitat to about two-thirds of the world’s tigers.

q:
Assertion (A): In the 14th century, Iltutmish constructed a large tank in Hauz Khas, Delhi.
Reason (R): The tank was built to supply water to the Siri Fort area.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Both statements are true and Reason (R) explains why Iltutmish constructed the Hauz Khas tank.

q:
Assertion (A): Meghalaya’s 200-year-old bamboo drip irrigation system uses heavy diesel pumps and concrete canals.
Reason (R): In this traditional system, stream and spring water is tapped using bamboo pipes and channelled down to drop 20–80 drops per minute at the plant site.
o: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is NOT the correct explanation of Assertion (A).
Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.
Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.
e: Assertion (A) is false because no diesel pumps or concrete canals are used; Reason (R) accurately describes how bamboo drip irrigation works.

q:
Read the passage: "Conservation strategies are not new in our country. We often ignore that in India, forests are also home to some of the traditional communities. In some areas of India, local communities are struggling to conserve these habitats along with government officials, recognising that only this will secure their own long-term livelihood. In Sariska Tiger Reserve, Rajasthan, villagers have fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act. In many areas, villagers themselves are protecting habitats and explicitly rejecting government involvement."

Why are local communities collaborating or actively leading habitat conservation?
o: Because only this will secure their own long-term livelihood and needs
e: The passage highlights that local communities recognise that conserving forest habitats alone will secure their own long-term livelihood.

q: Which law did the villagers in Sariska Tiger Reserve use to oppose mining activities?
e: Villagers in Sariska fought against mining by citing the Wildlife Protection Act.

q: What name did the inhabitants of five villages in Alwar district give to their 1,200-hectare community-protected forest?
e: They declared 1,200 hectares of forest as the Bhairodev Dakav "Sonchuri" with self-made rules against hunting.

q: What primary activity do local village-level institutions undertake under Joint Forest Management (JFM)?
o: Undertake protection activities mostly on degraded forest land managed by the forest department
e: Under JFM, local village institutions protect and restore degraded forest land managed by the forest department.

q: Which key conservation principle does the passage emphasise?
o: Local community participation is vital alongside official conservation efforts
Local people must be completely evicted from all forests
e: Cases like Sariska, Alwar and Chipko highlight that community participation is indispensable for effective ecological conservation.

q:
Read the passage: "Dams were traditionally built to impound rivers and rainwater that could be used later to irrigate agricultural fields. Today, dams are built not just for irrigation but for electricity generation, water supply for domestic and industrial uses, flood control, recreation, inland navigation and fish breeding. Hence, dams are now referred to as multi-purpose projects where the many uses of the impounded water are integrated with one another."

Why are modern dams referred to as "multi-purpose projects"?
o: Because impounded water integrates many uses: irrigation, electricity, water supply, flood control, recreation, navigation and fish breeding
e: Dams today integrate irrigation, power generation, flood control, water supply, inland navigation, recreation and fish breeding.

q: According to the passage, in which river basin does the Bhakra-Nangal project lie?
e: The passage specifically identifies the Sutlej-Beas river basin for the Bhakra-Nangal project.

q: Which two major functions does the Hirakud project integrate in the Mahanadi basin?
o: Conservation of water and flood control
e: As noted in the passage, the Hirakud project integrates conservation of water with flood control.

q: Who termed these multi-purpose dams as the "temples of modern India"?
e: Jawaharlal Nehru famously proclaimed dams as the "temples of modern India".

q: Why have large multi-purpose dams faced growing opposition and scrutiny in recent decades?
o: Obstruction of natural river/sediment flow, aquatic habitat fragmentation, mass displacement of local communities and sedimentation-induced flood risk
They are built only in deserts
e: Scrutiny stems from hampered natural/sediment flow, aquatic fragmentation, submergence of forests/soils, and mass displacement of local communities.

q:
Consider the following statements:
I. Enrichment plantation of teak monoculture damaged natural forests in South India.
II. Chir Pine plantations in the Himalayas replaced Himalayan oak and Rhododendron forests.
III. Colonial forest policies maximised India’s original floral biodiversity.
Which statements are correct?
e: Statements I and II are accurate per NCERT. Statement III is false because colonial commercial forestry severely damaged natural mixed biodiversity.

q:
Match the forest category with its prominent regional distribution in India:
A. High share of Reserved Forests — 1. Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan
B. Bulk under Protected Forests — 2. Kerala, Uttarakhand, Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh
C. High share of Unclassed Forests — 3. North-eastern states and parts of Gujarat
e: Reserved forests predominate in Kerala, Uttarakhand, Maharashtra, AP (A-2); Protected in Bihar, Haryana, Punjab, Rajasthan (B-1); Unclassed in NE states & Gujarat (C-3).

q: Which statement regarding Indian dams, rivers, or disputes is INCORRECT?
o: Koyna water diversion triggered disputes between Maharashtra, Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh
Hirakud dam is located on the Mahanadi
Rana Pratap Sagar and Kota Barrage are on the Chambal river
Salal project is located on the Luni river in Rajasthan
e: The Salal Project is built on the Chenab River in Jammu and Kashmir, not on the Luni River in Rajasthan.

q: A city receives 1,500 mm annual rainfall yet residents face severe water scarcity and rely on water tankers. Which explanation fits NCERT’s framework best?
o: Over-exploitation via private borewells, lack of rainwater harvesting/recharge on paved urban surfaces, and qualitative pollution of local rivers/lakes
1,500 mm rain contains no fresh water
e: Water scarcity can result from over-exploitation, excessive use, unequal access, lack of rainwater harvesting and qualitative pollution despite ample quantitative rainfall.

q:
Match the community conservation effort with its region/state:
1. Bhairodev Dakav "Sonchuri" — A. Tehri
2. Beej Bachao Andolan — B. Alwar (Rajasthan)
3. First JFM Resolution (1988) — C. Odisha
4. Worship of Mahua & Kadamba — D. Chota Nagpur
e: Bhairodev Dakav Sonchuri = Alwar (1-B); Beej Bachao = Tehri (2-A); First JFM = Odisha (3-C); Mahua/Kadamba = Chota Nagpur (4-D).

q:
Arrange the functioning steps of Rajasthan’s rooftop rainwater "tanka" system in logical sequence:
1. First spell of rain is discarded to clean the roof and pipes
2. Sloping roofs are connected via a PVC pipe to an underground tanka
3. Subsequent rain showers are collected and stored as clean "palar pani" till next monsoon
e: First sloping roofs connect via pipe to the tanka (2), then first rain flushes out dirt from roof/pipes (1), and subsequent showers fill the tanka cleanly (3).

q: Which socio-economic criticism of multi-purpose dams highlights inequity between winners and losers?
o: Local communities have to give up their land, livelihood and control over resources for the "greater good", while landowners, large farmers and industrialists reap benefits
Local tribes receive ownership of cities
Dams are built only in oceans
e: As noted in NCERT, local people often are not benefiting from these projects—large landowners, big farmers, industrialists and a few urban centres benefit while locals lose land and livelihood.

q:
Arrange the milestones in Indian forest & wildlife conservation chronologically (earliest to latest):
1. Launch of Project Tiger
2. First inclusion of six plant species under Wildlife Act
3. Implementation of Indian Wildlife (Protection) Act
4. First formal JFM resolution passed in Odisha
e: Wildlife Act (1972) → Project Tiger (1973) → JFM resolution in Odisha (1988) → Inclusion of 6 plant species (1991).

q: Arrange these four Indian Tiger Reserves/National Parks from WEST to EAST:
e: Sariska (Rajasthan, ~76°E) → Corbett (Uttarakhand, ~79°E) → Sundarbans (WB, ~88°E) → Manas (Assam, ~91°E).

q:
Match the historical hydraulic structure with its era:
1. Sringaverapura flood-water harvesting — A. 14th Century AD
2. Bhopal Lake — B. 1st Century BC
3. Hauz Khas Tank by Iltutmish — C. 11th Century AD
e: Sringaverapura = 1st Century BC (1-B); Bhopal Lake = 11th Century AD (2-C); Hauz Khas Tank = 14th Century AD (3-A).

q: Identify the FACTUALLY INCORRECT statement regarding India’s water resources:
o: Hydroelectricity contributes roughly 22% of India’s total electricity
Tehri Dam is built on the Bhagirathi river
Diversion channels in Western Himalayas are known as guls or kuls
Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) aims solely to desalinate seawater for mega ports
e: Jal Jeevan Mission aims to ensure assured potable piped water supply (55 litres/capita/day) to every rural household, not port desalination.

q: Which conclusion best captures NCERT’s perspective on India’s biological wealth and cultural practices?
o: Synergy between traditional cultural reverence (sacred groves, Bishnoi ethos) and modern statutory/community governance is key to conservation
e: NCERT highlights that traditional nature-worship and sacred groves alongside legal acts and community movements together preserve biodiversity.

q: What core lesson do Odisha’s JFM model and Alwar’s Bhairodev Dakav "Sonchuri" teach for resolving forest conservation conflicts?
o: Making local communities central stakeholders in decision-making and resource benefits achieves both ecological protection and human welfare
e: The chapter concludes that we still have to go a long way before local communities are at the centre-stage in decision-making; development must be people-centric, environment-friendly and economically rewarding.

q: How did the focus of the Narmada Bachao Andolan evolve over time?
o: Originally focused on environmental issues of trees submerged under dam water, it later refocused on enabling displaced citizens to get full rehabilitation facilities from the government
Started for coal mining, later turned to highways
e: Originally focused on environmental issues related to trees submerged under dam water, it recently refocused the aim to enable poor citizens, especially the oustees (displaced people), to get full rehabilitation facilities.

q: Which trio of projects from the NCERT Dams map is located along the Chambal river system?
o: Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar and Kota Barrage
e: According to the NCERT dams map, Gandhi Sagar, Rana Pratap Sagar and Kota Barrage lie on the Chambal river.

q: According to NCERT, which factors inflicted the greatest damage on Indian forests during the colonial period?
o: Expansion of railways, agriculture, commercial and scientific forestry and mining activities
e: The greatest damage inflicted on Indian forests was during the colonial period due to the expansion of the railways, agriculture, commercial and scientific forestry and mining activities.

q: According to the Forest Survey of India, approximately how much forest area was converted into agricultural land all over India between 1951 and 1980?
e: According to the Forest Survey of India, over 26,200 sq km of forest area was converted into agricultural land all over India between 1951 and 1980.

q: Comparing Rajasthan’s tankas and Karnataka’s Gendathur, what distinguishes successful community water harvesting?
o: They adapt to local rainfall, remain low-cost, prevent evaporation/contamination, and give households self-reliance
e: Rooftop harvesting and underground tankas are low-cost, evaporation-proof, community-managed methods providing household water security.

q: Which statement matches NCERT’s precise definition of a "Dam"?
o: A dam is a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment
A dam is merely an electricity turbine
A dam is an underground well
e: NCERT defines a dam as a barrier across flowing water that obstructs, directs or retards the flow, often creating a reservoir, lake or impoundment; "Dam" refers to the reservoir rather than the structure.

q:
Evaluate the statements regarding urbanisation and water scarcity in India:
1. Multiplying urban centres with dense populations added to water and energy requirements.
2. Housing colonies running private groundwater pumping devices aggravate groundwater depletion.
3. Urbanisation has eliminated chemical pollution in rivers.
Which are correct?
e: Statements 1 and 2 are true; Statement 3 is false because urban and industrial effluents severely pollute Indian rivers.

q: Which option correctly lists NCERT-highlighted Tiger Reserves from North, East, Central and South India respectively?
e: North: Corbett (Uttarakhand), East: Manas (Assam), Central: Bandhavgarh (MP), South: Periyar (Kerala).

q: According to Falkenmark, a Swedish expert, water stress occurs when water availability drops below which threshold?
e: According to Falkenmark, a Swedish expert, water stress occurs when water availability is less than 1,000 cubic metres per person.

q: Which statement accurately describes the ecological impacts of large reservoirs behind dams on surrounding vegetation and soil?
o: Existing vegetation and soils get submerged in the reservoir, leading to their decomposition over a period of time
Submerged trees grow twice as tall underwater
e: The reservoirs that are created on the floodplains also submerge the existing vegetation and soil leading to its decomposition over a period of time.

q: In addition to Chipko, which two movements are cited together in NCERT Forest & Wildlife Resources for demonstrating viable diversified crop production without synthetic chemicals?
e: Beej Bachao Andolan in Tehri and Navdanya are explicitly cited in NCERT for showing diversified chemical-free farming is viable.

q: Dams triggering earthquakes, water-borne diseases, pests and pollution from excessive water use highlight what broader lesson?
o: Mega river-engineering projects carry unintended geological, ecological and public-health hazards
e: Multi-purpose projects have also been observed to induce earthquakes, cause water-borne diseases and pests, and lead to pollution resulting from excessive use of water.

q: In traditional houses of Phalodi and Barmer, stored "palar pani" in underground tankas serves as the most reliable source of drinking water during which season?
o: Through dry months and summers until the next rains, when all other sources have dried up
Only in one week of January
e: Rainwater can be stored in the tankas till the next rainfall making it an extremely reliable source of drinking water when all other sources are dried up, particularly in the summers.

q: Why does NCERT highlight that Indian society traditionally holds trees like Peepal and Banyan sacred?
o: Certain societies revere a particular tree preserved from time immemorial due to cultural beliefs, protecting ecosystems and associated wildlife
e: Indian society comprises several cultures, each with its own traditional methods of conserving nature; trees like peepal and banyan are revered and protected.

q: Why is the bamboo drip irrigation system particularly suited to Meghalaya’s hill terrain?
o: Because gravity channels hill stream/spring water across steep terrain through bamboo pipes over hundreds of metres without soil erosion, releasing 20-80 drops/min at plant roots
Because Meghalaya is a flat desert
e: Using gravity on steep hills, stream water is diverted via bamboo channels to drop precisely at plant roots (20–80 drops/min), preventing waste and soil erosion.

q: Why do modern Indian water policies simultaneously promote both piped drinking supply (Jal Jeevan Mission) and rainwater harvesting / watershed conservation?
o: Because groundwater depletion and seasonal water stress threaten supply sustainability, requiring source recharge alongside piped distribution
e: Due to declining groundwater and spatial/temporal rainfall variation, long-term potable supply under JJM requires source sustainability through rainwater harvesting and recharge.

q: Whose profound words on the benevolence of trees ("A tree is a peculiar organism of unlimited kindness...") are quoted at the end of NCERT’s Forest and Wildlife Resources chapter?
e: Gautama Buddha (487 B.C.) is quoted saying a tree affords protection to all beings, offering shade even to the axeman who destroys it.
